We’re 10th-grade students from the School of Engineering named after Mirzo Ulugbek in Tashkent.

summary: KORAGON is a browser game where one to four players design and fly a satellite mission that solves a real problem on Earth: wildfires, drought, floods, air pollution, deforestation, sea level, urban heat and methane leaks. A guide, the 15th-century astronomer Mirzo Ulugʻbek of Samarkand, walks you through it. Four desks share one spacecraft: Flight Director, Engineer, Comms and Science. Each desk edits its own part of the design (orbit and rocket, parts and power, antennas and data, instruments and targets), so the team has to talk to each other. Parts are modelled on real NASA instruments such as Landsat, VIIRS, ECOSTRESS, NISAR and SWOT, and the meters for mass, power, cost and data react at once. Then you launch, fly through emergencies, and get a graded debrief that explains why the mission worked or failed. It runs in a browser with no account: solo, or in a team room with a four-letter code. A second mode puts the team on a Moon mission to the south pole, with a 1.28 second signal delay and a radio blackout behind the Moon. The goal is simple: let anyone feel the trade-offs of real mission design.
details:
KORAGON turns mission design into a team game. You pick a real problem on Earth, such as a wildfire emergency in California or drought around the shrinking Aral Sea. The planet turns to the place and outlines it. Then you build the satellite that would solve it.

How it works: four desks share one spacecraft. The Flight Director chooses the orbit and the rocket and commits the launch. The Engineer builds the bus, solar panels and batteries. Comms picks antennas, radios, memory and ground stations. Science chooses instruments and targets. What one desk changes, the others feel at once: a heavier instrument needs more power, more power needs bigger panels, and the rocket has a mass limit. Meters for mass, power, cost and data show the effect on every change. A 3D model of a real NASA spacecraft shows what kind of part you are picking.

After planning, a readiness check blocks launches that cannot work. Then the rocket launches, the mission flies, and emergencies appear that the team must decide on together. The debrief gives a grade and explains what helped and what hurt.

Benefits: players learn the real trade-offs between mass, power, cost, data and orbit, and learn that no single desk can finish a mission alone. A learner can play alone, holding all four desks. A team of four plays in a room with a four-letter code, no account needed. Levels range from Beginner (simple parts, friendly margins) to Expert (advanced parts, tight margins).

Tools: Next.js, React, TypeScript, three.js (the 3D rooms, globe and launch), Zustand, Supabase Realtime (team rooms), Vercel. Instrument classes and numbers come from NASA mission pages (see the NASA data page, https://koragon.vercel.app/nasa-data). The 3D spacecraft are NASA 3D Resources.

Creative: the guide is Mirzo Ulugʻbek, who mapped the stars from Samarkand, a link between our city and the sky. The mission-control room, the NASA-style launch, and a second mode on the Moon with a 1.28 s signal delay make the work feel real. Numbers that NASA does not publish are labelled as estimates.
